roots.context: We have found who the decomposers are, and what they need to eat dead things. Now we ask what rotting tells us about ourselves and the world.

deep_truth.truth: Both chapati pieces sat in the same air and caught the same mould spores. Only the damp piece grew mould and went soft. A mould digests food outside their body and soaks it up in water. So rotting is something living things do, and a dry leaf waits for the rain to be eaten.
deep_truth.habit: We say food 'goes bad' or 'spoils', as if time or the food itself did it. That hides the living things who are eating it. A dead leaf is not just falling apart. It is someone's meal, and the meal waits for water.
deep_truth.evidence: In the chapati test, the dry piece stayed clean all week in the same air as the damp piece. The damp piece in the fridge grew mould only slowly. In the Pickle Test, salted slices with plenty of water around them grew no mould, because the salt held the water.

three.who_am_i: Your body is made from food that was once other living things. Trillions of bacteria live in your gut and help digest your food.
three.what_is_life: Every living thing eats, and every living thing is eaten in the end. Decomposers make sure nothing is wasted.
three.what_is_this_world: The soil under a forest is mostly made by decomposers, from leaves, wood and animals that lived there before.

roots.thread: A badam leaf, a worm, a mould and a tulsi plant look like separate lives. But the leaf's material becomes the mould's threads, the worm's casts and the tulsi's new leaves. One store of material keeps passing from body to body. Each body is a short stop on that journey. This is a small picture of the One becoming the many: the same material, taking one shape after another.

teachings.teaching: From food all beings are born. By food they live. Into food they go when they depart.
teachings.link: A leaf grows from the soil, lives by the food it makes, and when it falls it becomes food for decomposers, and then for new plants.

teachings.teaching: All go to one place. All are of the dust, and all turn to dust again.
teachings.link: Decomposers turn every dead body, of a leaf, a worm or a person, back into soil.

teachings.teaching: All things grow and flourish, and each one returns to its root.
teachings.link: A fallen leaf really does return to the roots: decomposers turn it into nutrients that the tree's roots take in again.

science.text: When living things decompose, their atoms are not destroyed. They pass into the decomposers, the air and the soil, and are used again by new living things.
How much forest trees share with each other through fungus threads is still being argued about.

other_view.view: Decomposers are just feeding to stay alive, like any other living thing. The circle from leaf to soil to leaf is a pattern we notice, not a plan or a message. Calling it 'recycling' is a human way of describing it.

playtest: Every experiment, activity, game, challenge and project was walked through as if at home in a city flat, with the materials listed. Choices made: a homemade chapati is used instead of shop bread, because many shop breads contain a chemical that slows mould. All three chapati pieces sit in the same air for an hour first, so that the only difference is water or cold. The dry piece is crisped on a tawa or in the sun, because a soft chapati in a closed box can hold enough water to grow mould. Boxes stay closed so nobody breathes the spores. The Pickle Test uses a thick coat of salt, as in a real pickle, so the result is clear. The earthworm walk is outside the spine and marked for families with a garden or park, since worms are not reliably found in a flat.

how_we_found_out.story: In 1837, Charles Darwin had just come home from five years at sea. He visited his uncle, Josiah Wedgwood, at his farm in England. His uncle showed him something odd. Years before, burnt lime and cinders had been spread on top of some fields. Now they lay in a layer a few centimetres under the grass, as if the ground had grown over them. Most people thought worms were just pests, too small and weak to change a field. Darwin suggested that worms had done it, by swallowing soil below and leaving it on top as casts. Some people laughed. One writer said worms were far too feeble for such work. Darwin kept testing for about 40 years. He kept worms in pots in his study. He collected and weighed their casts. He watched them pull leaves into their burrows, usually by the narrow tip. He even had a piano played to them. They ignored the sound, but felt the shaking when their pot sat on the piano. In 1881 he wrote a whole book about worms. It showed that worms carry many tonnes of soil to the surface of each field every year, and slowly bury stones and old buildings.
how_we_found_out.who: Charles Darwin, with his uncle Josiah Wedgwood and his own children, who helped with the worm tests
how_we_found_out.when: 1837 (Darwin's first talk on worms) to 1881 (his book on worms)
how_we_found_out.wrong_idea: People thought worms were garden pests, far too small and weak to change the land. Darwin's measurements of casts and buried layers showed that worms slowly turn over and build the topsoil.
